template_name: C-Tactile Affective Touch Pathway for Architectural Surfaces
calibration_constraint: Bridge warrant for architectural surface parameters: CAPACITY (0.45) maximum per pre-panel review

mechanism_chain.process: Occupant makes contact with architectural surface (hand on railing, fingertips on wall, foot on floor, back against chair). Surface properties — roughness (Ra), thermal conductivity (λ), compliance (E), texture grain — are transduced by both Aβ mechanoreceptors (discriminative touch) and CT afferents (affective touch).
mechanism_chain.substrate: Peripheral nerve fibres in skin: Aβ (myelinated, fast) + CT (unmyelinated, slow, optimal velocity 1–10 cm/s)
mechanism_chain.source: Löken et al. (2009); Morrison et al. (2010)

data: C-tactile (CT) afferents are unmyelinated, slowly conducting fibres (0.5-2 m/s)
CT afferents respond maximally to stroking velocities 1-10 cm/s, peak ~3 cm/s
CT afferents are innervated primarily on hairy skin (forearm, back, leg), absent on glabrous skin (palm, sole)
Aβ mechanoreceptors are myelinated, fast-conducting (35-70 m/s), serve discriminative touch
Architectural contact (hand on railing, foot on floor) activates both channels but at different effective velocities
justification.backing: Löken et al. (2009) microelectrode recordings from CT afferents in humans; velocity tuning is directly measured. Morrison et al. (2010) on CT innervation density. Classic mechanoreceptor physiology from Sinclair (1967).
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.6 reflects direct human neural recording of CT afferent responses. MECHANISM warrant: CT fiber properties and velocity tuning are directly measured.
justification.rebuttal: CT density varies across body regions; architectural contact points (hands, feet, back) have lower CT densities than optimal laboratory sites (forearm). Individual variation in CT density exists.
competing_accounts: Aβ fibers alone mediate affective touch (refuted by CT lesion studies; CT afferents are necessary)
Affective touch is mediated by slow temporal integration of pressure (partially true but CT fiber tuning is the primary mechanism)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Löken & Morrison authorities

mechanism_chain.process: CT afferent firing rate encodes surface pleasantness: inverted-U response with peak at ~3 cm/s stroking velocity, moderate roughness (Ra 1–10 μm), skin-temperature warmth (~32°C surface), and moderate compliance
mechanism_chain.substrate: CT afferent unmyelinated C fibres → dorsal horn → spinothalamic tract
mechanism_chain.source: Löken et al. (2009); McGlone et al. (2014)

data: CT afferent firing rate peaks at ~3 cm/s stroking velocity
Pleasant touch is optimal at moderate roughness (Ra 1-10 μm)
Pleasant touch is optimal at skin-temperature warmth (~32°C surface)
Pleasant touch requires moderate compliance (not too hard, not too soft)
Inverted-U response profile: sub-threshold and supra-threshold velocities produce weaker responses
justification.backing: Löken et al. (2009) single-fiber recordings with velocity, texture, and temperature manipulation. McGlone et al. (2014) review of CT afferent physiology. Watkins et al. (2021) on palm CT-like responses.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.6 reflects controlled laboratory electrophysiology. MECHANISM warrant: CT encoding properties are directly measured under controlled conditions.
justification.rebuttal: Laboratory conditions (passive stroking) differ from architectural use (active contact, variable pressure, variable velocity). Field parameters (roughness, temperature, compliance) vary more than lab conditions.
competing_accounts: Affective response is purely top-down (cognitive expectation): refuted by CT fiber physiology independent of cognition
Temperature dominates pleasantness: refuted by velocity and texture effects demonstrated independently of temperature
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Löken et al. authority (direct physiology)

mechanism_chain.process: CT signal projects to posterior insular cortex, where it is processed as hedonic (pleasant/unpleasant) rather than discriminative. Posterior insula integrates CT input with interoceptive state (IC2 body budget) to generate an affective touch percept.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Posterior insular cortex → anterior insula (interoceptive integration) → orbitofrontal cortex (valuation)

data: CT afferent signals project to dorsal horn (spinal) then spinothalamic tract
Posterior insular cortex (piriform insular) receives CT projections
Posterior insula is site of hedonic valuation, not discriminative localization
Posterior insula integrates with anterior insula (interoception) and OFC (valuation)
This pathway is distinct from discriminative touch (SI cortex, Aβ-dominant)
justification.backing: Craig (2009) on insular cortex organization. Morrison (2016) on insular projections from CT afferents. Neuroimaging (PET, fMRI) localizes hedonic touch responses to posterior insula.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.55 reflects human neuroimaging and lesion evidence but less extensive than animal single-unit work. MECHANISM warrant: neural projection pathways are established from tracing and imaging.
justification.rebuttal: Insular cortex has multiple functional subdivisions; precise localization of CT response within posterior insula is debated. Individual variability in insular organization exists.
competing_accounts: Anterior insula alone mediates hedonic touch (refuted by focal posterior insula responses to CT stimulation)
OFC is the primary site (compatible; OFC receives insular input and generates final valuation)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Craig authority on insula; Morrison on CT projections

mechanism_chain.process: Pleasant architectural touch produces parasympathetic activation: reduced heart rate, reduced cortisol, increased positive affect. This is the haptic channel of the natural material stress reduction pathway.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Insular cortex → autonomic regulation → parasympathetic shift

data: CT stimulation (pleasing touch) reduces heart rate (parasympathetic marker)
CT stimulation reduces cortisol (stress hormone)
CT stimulation increases positive affect (self-report, facial EMG)
Effect is mediated by insular cortex connections to nucleus accumbens and periaqueductal gray (PAG)
Effect is attenuated in patients with damage to insular cortex or disrupted vagal afferents
justification.backing: McGlone et al. (2014) on autonomic effects of C-tactile stimulation. Morrison (2016) review of hedonic touch pathway. Walker et al. (2017) on touch and stress reduction.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.45 reflects field studies and physiological correlates but causality is inferred. CAPACITY warrant: functional effects are measured but the complete pathway is partially inferred.
justification.rebuttal: Autonomic responses could be mediated by expectation (top-down) rather than CT signals alone. Individual differences in parasympathetic tone could moderate effects. Architectural contact is less controlled than laboratory stroking.
competing_accounts: Stress reduction is purely psychological (expectation): refuted by CT-mediated effects in non-human primates lacking explicit expectations
Sympathetic arousal masks CT benefit: partially true; high baseline arousal might occlude parasympathetic shift

ct_optimal_velocity.interpretation: CT afferents fire maximally at gentle stroking velocities. Architectural contact modes (gripping, pressing, walking) produce lower effective velocities than laboratory stroking, reducing CT activation.

body_site_attenuation_factors.interpretation: Hedonic response magnitude relative to forearm reference. Palm and fingertips have lower CT density but some CT-like responses (Watkins et al., 2021). Sole primarily thermal/compliance rather than CT.

surface_roughness_preference.interpretation: Moderate roughness is preferred; extreme smooth or rough is aversive. Wood (Ra ~5–15 μm) is near optimal; polished metal (Ra < 0.1 μm) is too smooth; rough concrete (Ra > 100 μm) is too rough.

thermal_conductivity_preference.interpretation: Low thermal conductivity = warm to touch = pleasant CT activation. High conductivity = cold to touch = reduced CT firing and negative affect.

visual_expectation_pathway.interpretation: Seeing warm, natural materials (wood grain, natural stone texture) generates anticipatory pleasant touch expectation via crossmodal correspondence (Spence). This operates even without actual contact.

age_group.effect: CT afferent density and conduction may decline with age, but the hedonic valuation pathway in insular cortex is preserved. Net effect: slightly attenuated CT activation but preserved affective response.

neuropathy.effect: Peripheral neuropathy (diabetic, chemotherapy-induced) damages CT afferents. Haptic pleasure from architectural surfaces is reduced or absent. These populations rely more heavily on visual and olfactory channels.

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: CT afferent signals are integrated with interoceptive state in posterior/anterior insula. Pleasant touch under body budget balance produces positive affect; pleasant touch under body budget deficit may be attenuated or reinterpreted (the same warm wood surface that is comforting when well-nourished may be irrelevant when hungry or in pain).
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: Voluntary touch (self-initiated contact with a surface) produces stronger CT hedonic response than involuntary contact (bumping into a surface, forced contact with a railing). Perceived control over the touch interaction amplifies the pleasant affect.

material_warmth_index.interpretation: Composite of thermal conductivity and surface texture grain. Wood scores highest (~0.85); cork (~0.90); natural fibre textile (~0.80); stone (~0.30); metal (~0.10).

touch_opportunity_density.interpretation: Number of touchable surfaces per unit path length. Railings, door handles, seating surfaces, wall textures at hand height all contribute. Higher density → more CT activation opportunities per journey.

Touch-based affect contributes to material identity formation
